summary: Sand City may be one of the smallest incorporated cities in California — just 374 residents spread across 2.9 square miles of former dune land along Monterey Bay — yet it generates an outsized volume of commercial activity, which explains the eye-popping per-capita crime figures: a larceny rate north of 53,000 per 100,000 is almost entirely a function of the big-box retail and outlet shopping centers that draw thousands of non-residents daily through a city whose actual population barely fills a large apartment building. Wedged between Seaside and Monterey on a strip of coastal sand flats, the terrain is low, wind-sculpted, and dotted with remnant dune habitat, giving way to unobstructed Pacific views and cool, remarkably stable weather — average highs hover near 64°F year-round with eight hours of daily sunshine, meaning fog burns off but true heat almost never arrives. The housing math is severe: a median home value near $986,000 against a median household income of roughly $78,000 produces a price-to-income ratio above 12:1, pushing ownership well beyond what local earnings alone support, while median rent at $1,964 consumes about 30% of that same income. The city functions less as a self-contained community and more as a commercial corridor with a handful of residential pockets — a place defined by the tension between its enormous retail footprint and its almost nonexistent residential population.
